name: AAWC World Heavyweight Championship
notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
epitaph: The AAWC's own top belt, and the one whose record breaks in half. Its earliest trace is its own disappearance: on 24 October 1993, at the CSWA's LAST CALL II, "AAWC World Champion Hot Shot" carried it into a six-man IRONMAN of CHAMPIONS that merged the IWCCW World title, the AAWC World title and a ten-title Unified Championship into one belt, and Hornet won the final. Three years later the AAWC is billing an AAWC World Heavyweight Championship again, and nothing held says how it came back. In that second life Marcus Price held it and lost it weeks before Oktoberfest '96, in a triangle match against Dr. Silver and "Superstar" Scotty Michaels that he went into with his own finisher suspended: Silver had filed a protest with the AAWC offices calling the Fashion Statement a blatant chokehold, the office suspended the hold pending an investigation, and the referee stopped Price using it. Price's answer was to apply it to the fed's President at ringside. Silver walked out of that match with the belt and was still carrying it into the New Orleans SuperDome, where he spent the night filling other people's tag matches with his own men and steering the Television title into the hands of a wrestler he had apparently been running since the man's first night. Whether Silver ever lost it is not recorded, but by the summer of 1997 the belt was moving fast: "Superstar" Scotty Michaels was newly crowned on 9 July, and inside a fortnight Steve Masters — a former champion himself — took it off him at World War Games 3 in Wembley Stadium on a stipulation added mid-match, with the board's own headline wondering whether Michaels could begin a third reign in two months. Masters is still champion at the last word anywhere held.

name: AAWC United States Heavyweight Championship
notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
epitaph: The AAWC's secondary singles belt, and the one with the longest memory in the fed's own commentary. Marcus Price held it in the mid-1990s and lost it to Dr. Silver, who "outsmarted Price two years ago to beat him for the very same AAWC United States title"; Mike Randalls held it at some point too, billed as a former champion in his own right on a night the record does not date. Price won it back in Pittsburgh the week before Oktoberfest '96 and was booked to defend it on both of that event's nights — first against Randalls, then against "Marvelous" Mike Chain. The Randalls defence is the one the record holds: a bloodbath in which Randalls jabbed a broken table leg into his own forehead to shake off the Fashion Statement, and Price tried to walk up the aisle and was sent back by the fed's own President. The one surviving copy of the card ends mid-count on a Price small package, so who left New Orleans with the belt is not recorded. Nine months after that, in July 1997, the belt was on Anarky, booked to defend it at Wembley Stadium in a rematch with "Marvelous" Mike Chain.

name: AAWC Television Championship
notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
epitaph: "Lethal" Lex Taylor held the AAWC Television title in what the fed's own broadcast called a vice-grip, broken once by Big Mack and regained in a tag team rematch. It came off him at Oktoberfest '96 in a triangle match against Xavier Virile and Bloodhunt, under a stipulation that the first man to pin anybody won it. Taylor had the match won — he hit the Lex Plex on Virile and raised his own hand — but Bloodhunt had tagged himself in a half-second earlier, put Taylor down with the Headshot, tagged Virile's arm and rolled him, barely conscious, on top of the champion. Dr. Silver's entire group came to the ring afterwards, and Silver handed the belt to Virile himself in exchange for a bottle of water: the night the AAWC's own commentary worked out that Virile had been Silver's from day one. Nine months later it was around Troy Windham's waist, booked into a four corners defence at World War Games 3 and billed on a rival promotion's own card as the belt he carried into a World title match there.

name: AAWC Universal Tag Team Championship
notes: Attested by the fed's own Oktoberfest '96 (Night 1) card of 25 October 1996 (promotions/nfw/archive/news-1996-10-25-aawc-oktoberfest-96-night-1.html).
epitaph: The AAWC's own tag team championship, held across the fed's two surviving cards by two different teams and never once seen changing hands. In August 1995 it was on THE ARMED FORCES, Battleship and Submarine, led by their manager TTL, who kept it at Cameron Indoor Arena when the referee ruled a double disqualification on a challenge by ARROGANCE — Joey Melton and Peyton Wright, with Teri Melton at ringside — after Steven Flair and GUNS both got involved. By Oktoberfest '96 it was on "Showtime" Shawn Matthews and "Flannel Animal" Kurt Taylor, booked to defend against the Dirty Rotten Scoundrels, a team the broadcast booth spent the first night pretending to be frightened of. The Vegas Connection had come close to the belts earlier that year, and the Untouchables won their way into the second night's match on the first. When and from whom either reign began, and whether either ended, is not in the surviving record.

name: AAWC Universal Heavyweight Championship
notes: Attested by the AAWC's own card of 5 August 1995, AAWC's UNDER NEW OWNERSHIP, served in the CSWA wing (promotions/cswa/archive/aawcs-under-new-ownership-1995-08-05.html), and by the CSWA's own Unified World Heavyweight Championship history (promotions/cswa/archive/unified-world-heavyweight-championship-history-1997.html). It is named on neither of the Oktoberfest '96 card's own three title matches; whether it was still active in October 1996 is not in the record.
epitaph: The belt the AAWC carried through 1995, and the one its own record only ever shows being defended against outsiders. "Mr. Magnificent" Tom Adler won it at WrestleFest, the night the fed's presidency was sold out from under Robert Schmid, and defended it that August at Cameron Indoor Arena in a steel cage against GUNS, with GUNS' own Enterprises World Heavyweight title also on the line — a match decided when Adler dropped down the far side of the cage while a commentator held GUNS off the floor on his shoulders. Adler left with both belts. Three months later, at Thanksgiving Weekend 1995, Hornet beat him and took the Universal title away as well. The AAWC's own Oktoberfest '96 card, thirteen months after that, names four championships and this is not one of them.

name: AAWC Unified Championship
notes: Attested by a CSWA retrospective on the Hornet/GUNS feud (promotions/cswa/archive/cswa-spotlight-hornet-vs-guns-1998.html), which describes it as "created from a previous merge of three of the AAWC's lesser titles" and records its own end: at WrestleFest '95 it was merged with the AAWC World Title to create the AAWC Universal Championship.
epitaph: A belt built out of three other belts and then folded into a fourth. The AAWC merged three of its own lesser championships into a Unified Championship, and Hornet took it from Mike Randalls at the fed's own World War Games in March 1995 — a win GUNS answered by attacking him, which is where a three-year feud across four promotions started. Two months later the AAWC merged this title with its own World Championship at WrestleFest '95 to crown a single Universal Champion, in a round robin the surviving account describes as GUNS, Hornet, Dr. Silver and Flic Rair, the first man to beat his three opponents in consecutive matches taking the belt. Nobody else is recorded as holding it.
